clinicalPearls: Hemochromatosis is variably classified as a metabolic or storage disease; the common autosomal recessive form is related to the HFE gene (Harrison 22e p.2062).

Up to 10% of the population is heterozygous for one HFE mutation, so clinical prevalence might be as high as 1 in 500, though observed rates are lower because of limited (incomplete) penetrance (Harrison 22e p.2062).
Increased iron in the skin in types 1 and 2 hemochromatosis stimulates melanin pigment production and leads to the classic bronze color (Harrison 22e p.443).

Systemic iron overload is diagnosed from serum iron and transferrin saturation, with thresholds noted around >60% in men and >45-50% in women; ferritin and transferrin saturation are the main usable laboratory biomarkers of iron status (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.805).

MRI is used to quantitate iron stores in the liver and heart; for cardiac iron overload the diagnosis is made principally by MRI, and endomyocardial biopsy (Prussian blue stain) is not usually needed (Harrison 22e p.2062).
When diagnosed early, hemochromatosis can often be managed by repeated phlebotomy to remove iron (Harrison 22e p.2062).

Hepcidin-regulating proteins HFE, transferrin receptor 2, and hemojuvelin, whose mutations cause different forms of hemochromatosis, normally contribute to hepcidin upregulation; impaired hepcidin signaling allows excess iron entry into plasma (Harrison 22e p.805).

There is no regulated mechanism for iron excretion; physiologic iron loss occurs only through cell desquamation and menses, which is why unregulated absorption produces progressive overload (Harrison 22e p.805).
harrison.pathophysiology: Systemic iron homeostasis is controlled by hepcidin, a hepatocyte-derived peptide that blocks the iron exporter ferroportin, limiting iron flux from duodenal enterocytes, recycling macrophages, and storing hepatocytes. High plasma/liver iron normally raises hepcidin via the BMP-SMAD pathway, with HFE, transferrin receptor 2, and hemojuvelin contributing to hepcidin upregulation. Mutations in these genes (most commonly HFE) lead to inappropriately low hepcidin, increased iron absorption, and rising transferrin saturation. Because no regulated route of iron excretion exists, iron accumulates progressively. When transferrin saturation exceeds ~60%, non-transferrin-bound iron (NTBI) appears in the circulation and is taken up by liver, pancreas, and heart, driving parenchymal injury. In the heart, excess iron deposits in the perinuclear compartment of cardiomyocytes, disrupting intracellular architecture and mitochondrial function (Harrison 22e p.805, p.2062).
additionalDifferentials: Secondary (acquired) iron overload from chronic transfusion in hemoglobinopathies/thalassemia (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.821)
Other metabolic causes of skin hyperpigmentation: porphyria cutanea tarda, vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, pellagra, malabsorption/Whipple's disease (Harrison 22e p.443)
nonInfectiousMimics: Other causes of restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy; hemochromatosis is listed among restrictive cardiomyopathies but often presents clinically as a dilated cardiomyopathy (Harrison 22e p.2062)
Other chronic liver diseases progressing to cirrhosis (alcohol, viral hepatitis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis) (Harrison 22e p.702)
additionalInvestigations: Transferrin saturation (serum iron / total iron-binding capacity) as a key screening test for iron overload (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.805)
Serum ferritin to assess body iron stores (Harrison 22e p.805)
MRI quantitation of hepatic and cardiac iron stores (Harrison 22e p.2062)
Genetic testing for HFE mutations (the gene underlying the common autosomal recessive form) (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.702)
Endomyocardial biopsy with Prussian blue iron stain (reserved; not usually needed when MRI is available) (Harrison 22e p.2062)
redFlags: Hemochromatosis (HFE germline mutations) is a recognized risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, typically via cirrhosis (Harrison 22e p.702)
Progression to cirrhosis from hepatic iron loading (Harrison 22e p.2062)
Cardiomyopathy from cardiac siderosis, which may cause heart failure or arrhythmia (Harrison 22e p.2062)
Markedly increased susceptibility to Vibrio vulnificus sepsis (primary sepsis develops most often in patients with cirrhosis or hemochromatosis) (Harrison 22e p.1373)

Increased susceptibility to Yersinia (Y. enterocolitica / Y. pseudotuberculosis) septicemia, with iron overload providing accessible iron; iron chelators such as desferrioxamine can precipitate Yersinia infection (Harrison 22e p.1392)
harrison.prognosis: If diagnosed early, iron overload can often be removed by repeated phlebotomy, and cardiac function can improve with iron removal provided myocyte loss and replacement fibrosis are not too severe. Late disease carries the burden of established cirrhosis (with hepatocellular carcinoma risk) and irreversible cardiac and endocrine damage (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.702).
pitfalls: Incomplete penetrance: many HFE mutation carriers never develop clinical iron-overload disease, so genotype does not equal phenotype, and additional genetic and environmental factors (e.g., alcohol) modify expression (Harrison 22e p.2062).
Hemochromatosis may present clinically as a dilated cardiomyopathy even though it is categorized among restrictive cardiomyopathies (Harrison 22e p.2062).

Iron chelation therapy itself (e.g., desferrioxamine) can supply accessible iron to Yersinia and impair neutrophil function, precipitating Yersinia septicemia in iron-overloaded patients (Harrison 22e p.1392).
management: Deplete iron stores with regular therapeutic phlebotomy until iron indices normalise, then continue lifelong maintenance venesection
Use iron chelation with deferoxamine or deferasirox in patients who cannot tolerate phlebotomy, such as those with anaemia or severe cardiac disease
Advise dietary and lifestyle measures: avoid iron and vitamin C supplements, moderate alcohol intake and avoid raw shellfish given Vibrio vulnificus susceptibility
Monitor iron status with serum ferritin and transferrin saturation to guide venesection, and quantify hepatic and cardiac iron with MRI
Manage established organ complications: treat diabetes mellitus, replace pituitary and gonadal hormones for hypogonadism, treat the cardiomyopathy and manage the arthropathy
Surveil cirrhotic patients for hepatocellular carcinoma with periodic liver imaging
Offer HFE genetic testing, genetic counselling and screening of first-degree relatives given autosomal recessive inheritance
